notes:
Below are the verse‑by‑verse notes, drawn from the pages found. Each point is tagged with its source URL. Where a tradition’s own teachers were found, their distinctive reading is noted; where a search returned nothing, that is stated.

---

### v. 1 – “Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and earth had passed away, and the sea was no more.”

- **The “new” is qualitative, not chronological.** The Greek *kainos* means “new in character, fresh,” not merely recent in time. It is a better heaven and earth replacing the old. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-21/; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/21.htm)
- **This is the eternal state, not the Millennium.** Walvoord notes the absence of sea is decisive: millennial passages repeatedly mention seas and bodies of water (Ps 72:8; Ezek 47; Zech 14:8), but here “there was no more sea.” Most commentators therefore place the vision after the Millennium. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-21/)
- **The sea has symbolic weight.** In Jewish thought the sea represented separation and evil; in Revelation the beast rose from the sea (13:1) and the sea gave up its dead (20:13). Ellicott sees the sea as the “restless, tumultuous ocean” of evil and rebellion — now gone. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-21/; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/21.htm)
- **The Pulpit Commentary** notes a two‑fold interpretation: some take “no more sea” literally (the physical sea no longer exists); others take it symbolically as the absence of restless, unstable wicked nations. (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/21.htm)
- **Gill** (historic Baptist) reads the new heaven and earth as the literal, renewed creation purged by the conflagration, fit for the habitation of Christ and the saints during the thousand‑year reign (Rev 20). He notes the sea may still exist but have lost its turbulent, salty, deadly qualities. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/revelation/21.htm)

### v. 2 – “I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.”

- **The city is the Church glorified.** The Pulpit Commentary, Ellicott and Gill all identify the holy city with the Church of God, now perfected. Ellicott: “The city is also the bride… both images are familiar.” (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/21.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/21.htm)
- **The city descends from God — it is not man’s achievement.** It is a gift, prepared by God, not built by human effort. Enduring Word: “This city is not and never can be the achievement of man.” (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-21/)
- **Lutheran (1517.org):** The city‑as‑bride imagery points to the church’s mystical union with Christ. The vision offers deep comfort now by directing faith toward the future consummation. Christ “will have His church as His own.” (1517.org/articles/epistle-revelation-211-17-easter-5-series-c-2025)
- **Gill** uniquely places this entire vision during the thousand‑year reign on a renewed earth, not the final eternal state. The descent from heaven is a “local descent of all the saints with Christ from the third heaven into the air” to reign on earth. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/revelation/21.htm)
- **On studylight.org**, a dispensational note argues the New Jerusalem is not identical with the church; it is a real city that encompasses both Israel and the church — the corporate dwelling of all the redeemed. (studylight.org/commentary/revelation/21-2.html)

### v. 3 – “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them…”

- **The covenant promise fulfilled.** All the sources see this as the ultimate fulfilment of the covenant formula (“I will be their God, they shall be My people” — Lev 26:11‑12; Ezek 37:27). The Pulpit Commentary notes the plural “peoples” points to the catholic (universal) nature of the New Jerusalem gathering many nations. (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/21.htm)
- **“Tabernacle” imagery is deliberate.** Ellicott insists we should retain “tabernacle” rather than merely “dwell,” because it recalls the tent‑presence of God with Israel. The difference from Rev 7:15: there God tabernacled *over* them; here He tabernacles *with* them. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/21.htm)
- **Spurgeon** (cited by Enduring Word): The greatest glory of Eden was not its walks or fruit but that “the Lord God walked in the garden in the cool of the day.” Heaven restores that intimacy. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-21/)
- **Gill** sees this as Christ’s personal, bodily presence reigning among His saints — not merely spiritual presence, but “in person.” (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/revelation/21.htm)

### v. 4 – “He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, for the former things have passed away.”

- **“Every tear”** (not “all tears”) is the more accurate, tender rendering. Ellicott: “and so possess the promise in its true and tender form.” (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/21.htm)
- **The six negatives mark a complete reversal of the Fall.** Ellicott lists them: no sea, no tears, no death, no mourning, no crying, no pain. The “former things” that pass away are all the effects of sin. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/21.htm)
- **Enduring Word** (citing Walvoord) warns against guilt‑manipulation: the tears wiped away are not tears of remorse in heaven; the emphasis is on God’s comfort, not the saints’ regret. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-21/)
- **Gill:** No more natural death, no more persecution unto death, no more spiritual deadness, and the second death has no power over the saints. He quotes a Jewish source: “there is no death in the world to come.” (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/revelation/21.htm)
- **Lutheran (1517.org):** This is the heart of the good news for suffering believers — the death of death itself, providing “deep comfort and hope in the present.” (1517.org/articles/epistle-revelation-211-17-easter-5-series-c-2025)

### v. 5 – “Behold, I make all things new… Write this down, for these words are faithful and true.”

- **Present‑tense force.** The One on the throne says “I am making all things new” (present tense). This is the consummation of a renewal already begun (2 Cor 5:17). Ellicott: “out of the world, so full of distress and tears… will emerge the glad new world.” (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/21.htm; enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-21/)
- **Redeemed man surpasses innocent man.** Enduring Word notes that redeemed man is greater than unfallen Adam; we gain more in Christ than we lost in Adam. God’s perfect state is redemption, not mere innocence. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-21/)
- **Spurgeon** preached a whole sermon on this verse (“A New Creation”): the new creation is entirely God’s work; man contributes nothing. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/revelation-21.html)
- **Gill** identifies the speaker as Christ (because He calls Himself Alpha and Omega), listing ten things Jewish tradition says God will make new in the world to come, several matching this chapter. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/revelation/21.htm)
- **The command to “Write”** suggests John was so overwhelmed he forgot to record the words — they must be preserved because they are reliable. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-21/; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/21.htm)

### v. 6 – “It is done! I am the Alpha and the Omega… To the thirsty I will give freely from the spring of the water of life.”

- **“It is done” = “They have come to pass.”** Ellicott notes this is the second time in Revelation that “It is done” is declared (first at the completion of God’s wrath in 16:17). Now it marks the completion of all things new. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/21.htm)
- **“Alpha and Omega”** brackets the book; God’s eternal, unchanging nature guarantees every promise. (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/21.htm)
- **Thirst and drinking as a picture of faith.** Spurgeon: “There is perhaps no better representation of faith in all the Word of God than that. To drink is to receive… Drinking is such a remarkably easy thing.” Salvation is freely given, not earned. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-21/)
- **Gill:** The “water of life” promise echoes Isaiah 55:1 and John 7:37‑38 — the gift is without money and without price. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/revelation/21.htm)

### v. 7 – “The one who overcomes will inherit all things, and I will be his God, and he will be My son.”

- **The overcomer is defined by faith.** Enduring Word points to 1 John 5:4‑5: the victory that overcomes the world is faith in Jesus. It is not moral perfection but trust. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-21/)
- **Individual application.** Ellicott notes the general promise of v.3 is now repeated “more individually.” The echo of the letters to the seven churches (Rev 2–3) is deliberate. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/21.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary** says this promise, first made to David concerning Solomon (2 Sam 7:14), found its messianic fulfilment in Christ (Heb 1:5), and is now fulfilled in the members of Christ. (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/21.htm)
- **Gill:** “All things” means the new heaven and earth and all the glories of the New Jerusalem. The relationship “I will be his God, and he shall be My son” is the greatest inheritance. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/revelation/21.htm)

### v. 8 – “But to the cowardly and unbelieving and abominable… their place will be in the lake that burns with fire and sulfur. This is the second death.”

- **“Cowardly” heads the list — why?** Leon Morris (quoted by Enduring Word): “John is not speaking of natural timidity, but of that cowardice which in the last resort chooses self and safety before Christ.” It is the fear of man that leads to apostasy. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-21/)
- **Ellicott** sees the sins arranged in pairs: cowardice and unbelief go together (Deut 20:1‑8; Matt 8:26); abomination and murder; fornication and sorcery; idolatry and falsehood. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/21.htm)
- **The list does not mean one lapse damns.** Ellicott adds: “Sin indeed excludes from the city, but it is sin loved, sin unrepented of, which alone can close the gate.” (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/21.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary** notes the change in construction mid‑verse: the fate of these sinners is not just punitive but is their chosen “part” — the second death is what they inherit instead of the first resurrection. (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/21.htm)
- **Gill** places this warning within the millennial framework: those excluded from the thousand‑year reign suffer the lake of fire. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/revelation/21.htm)

### v. 9 – “Then one of the seven angels with the seven bowls… ‘Come, I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb.’”

- **Deliberate parallel with the harlot vision.** The same kind of angel who showed John the judgment of the great harlot (Rev 17:1) now shows him the bride. The Pulpit Commentary calls this “the great contrast.” (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/21.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/21.htm)
- **The bride is a city.** Enduring Word notes some wonder whether the New Jerusalem is merely a symbol for the Church. The answer: the city is literal but called the bride because it is where all God’s people dwell. The city and the bride are associated to convey beauty, not to deny the city’s reality. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-21/)
- **Lutheran (1517.org):** The Holy Spirit mixes metaphors freely — the Lamb has a wife, the wife is a city, the city has apostles, the temple is the Lord God and the Lamb. The preacher should not be afraid to do the same, for the point is the mystical union of Christ and the Church. (1517.org/articles/epistle-revelation-219-14-21-27-easter-6-series-c)

### v. 10 – “And he carried me away in the Spirit to a mountain great and high, and showed me the holy city…”

- **A mountain for perspective.** Ellicott sees symbolism: “The glimpse of God’s coming glories is best gained from the consecrated heights of self‑surrender and prayer.” The tempter took Jesus to a high mountain to show the world’s kingdoms; the angel takes John to show the city whose builder is God. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/21.htm)
- **Gill:** The mountain represents not merely a vantage point but the exalted state in which divine revelations are received. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/revelation/21.htm)

### v. 11 – “shining with the glory of God. Its radiance was like a most precious jewel, like a jasper, as clear as crystal.”

- **The Shekinah glory.** All commentators agree this is the abiding presence of God — the same glory that filled the tabernacle (Ex 40:34) and temple (1 Kgs 8:11). The “jasper” is probably the diamond, clear and brilliant. (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/21.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/21.htm)
- **Transparency = unobstructed glory.** Enduring Word (citing Walvoord): the constant mention of transparency throughout the chapter “indicates that the city is designed to transmit the glory of God in the form of light without hindrance.” (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-21/)

### vv. 12‑14 – The wall, twelve gates, twelve tribes, twelve foundations, twelve apostles.

- **The gates face all directions — universal access.** Ellicott: “The gates lie open to all quarters; there is no refusal of admission to any people.” The arrangement may recall the wilderness camp (Numbers 2) or Ezekiel 48. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/21.htm)
- **The wall is for definition and exclusion, not defence.** No enemies remain; the wall marks the city as distinct and indicates that some are outside. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-21/)
- **Israel and the Church together.** The gates bear the names of the twelve tribes; the foundations bear the names of the twelve apostles. The Old and New Testament people of God are united in one city. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-21/; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/21.htm)
- **Angels at the gates** signify absolute security. The Pulpit Commentary: angels still fulfilling their guardian role, though no assault is expected. (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/21.htm)
- **Apostolic foundation.** Ellicott notes complete harmony with Ephesians 2:20 — the Church is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets. The argument that St John could not have written this because he refers to “the twelve apostles” (including himself) is dismissed as confusion about symbolic language. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/21.htm)
- **Gill:** The twelve apostles are the twelve original disciples of the Lamb, their names permanently inscribed as a testimony to their foundational role. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/revelation/21.htm)

### vv. 15‑16 – The measuring: 12,000 stadia, length = width = height.

- **A golden measuring rod** signifies the heavenly character of the work. The measuring shows the city’s vast scale and perfect symmetry. (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/21.htm)
- **A perfect cube or pyramid.** The city is either a cube or a pyramid. A cube recalls the Holy of Holies (1 Kgs 6:20), also cubical. This suggests the entire city is the Most Holy Place — all inhabitants are priests in God’s immediate presence. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-21/; biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/21.htm)
- **12,000 stadia ≈ 2,400 km (1,500 miles) on each side.** The size is enormous (roughly the footprint of the moon). Leon Morris: “A city of this size is too large for the imagination to take in. John is certainly conveying the idea of splendour. And, more importantly, that of room for all.” (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-21/)
- **Figurative intent.** The Pulpit Commentary: “The account given is that of a vision, and not of a reality, and therefore there is no need to attempt to reduce the enormous dimensions.” (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/21.htm)

### v. 17 – “And he measured its wall to be 144 cubits, by the human measure the angel was using.”

- **144 cubits ≈ 65 metres (216 feet).** This is a relatively modest height compared with the city’s own height (12,000 stadia). Two explanations are offered: (a) the city sits on a great mountain and the wall is on top of it; (b) the wall’s modest height symbolises that the most inconsiderable wall is sufficient when only the pure may enter (Düsterdieck). (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/21.htm)
- **The number 144** (12 × 12) signals completeness, matching the 144,000 sealed in Rev 7. (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/21.htm)
- **“Measure of a man, that is, of an angel”** — in this case the angel uses ordinary human cubits, not some mysterious angelic measure. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-21/)

### vv. 18‑21 – Jasper wall, gold city, twelve gemstone foundations, pearl gates, golden street.

- **The materials are both literal and symbolic.** Enduring Word: we should take them as literal representations, yet they express realities we cannot fully grasp now. The use of riches conveys the immense value of what God has prepared. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-21/)
- **The twelve gemstones** may echo the High Priest’s breastplate (Ex 28:15‑21). Precise identification of each stone in modern terms is difficult, but the impression is one of unending, staggering beauty. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-21/; biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/21.htm)
- **Transparency everywhere** (pure gold “as clear as glass”) signals that the city is designed to transmit God’s glory without obstruction. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-21/)
- **Each gate is a single pearl.** Enduring Word notes a secondary symbolism: pearls come from an unclean animal (oyster, Lev 11:10), and may signify that the redeemed from among the Gentiles, once considered unclean, can now pass through the gates — cleansed by God. This also recalls the “pearl of great price” (Matt 13:45‑46). (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-21/)
- **The street is singular** — not one street among many, but the whole collective material of the city’s public spaces is pure gold. (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/21.htm)

### v. 22 – “But I saw no temple in the city, because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple.”

- **No temple, because the whole city is the Holy of Holies.** The Pulpit Commentary: all the redeemed are within the sanctuary, all are now priests (cf. Rev 20:6). The inner shrine (ναός) is unnecessary because God’s presence fills everything. (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/21.htm)
- **The temple is not removed but expanded.** Enduring Word (citing Alford): “The inhabitants need no place of worship or sacrifice, the object of all worship being present, and the great sacrifice Himself being there.” Everything and every place is holy. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-21/)
- **Lutheran (1517.org):** This recalls Jesus’ own words about the temple and points to the church’s consummation in Christ. No created structure mediates God’s presence any longer. (1517.org/articles/epistle-revelation-219-14-21-27-easter-6-series-c)
- **Gill** sees this as consistent with the millennial reign on earth: public worship, ministry and ordinances that existed in the church age will cease; the Lord God and the Lamb will be the temple in person. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/revelation/21.htm)

### v. 23 – “And the city has no need of sun or moon to shine on it, because the glory of God illuminates the city, and the Lamb is its lamp.”

- **Fulfilment of Isaiah 60:19‑20.** The Pulpit Commentary: “The sun shall be no more thy light by day… but the Lord shall be unto thee an everlasting Light.” John sees the prophetic word fully realised. (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/21.htm)
- **No distinction between God and the Lamb as light.** Both are equally the source. Ellicott: “No distinction is to be made between God and the Lamb; both are the Light (cf. John 1:5).” (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/21.htm)
- **Light = joy, beauty and knowledge.** Enduring Word: in Scripture light and joy go together; without light there is no beauty; light speaks of knowledge — in heaven we will know Him as He knows us. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-21/)

### v. 24 – “By its light the nations will walk, and into it the kings of the earth will bring their glory.”

- **“The nations” are the redeemed from every people group, not unbelievers.** Although the KJV adds “of them which are saved” (not in the best manuscripts), the sense is correct: these are the redeemed described in Rev 7:9 — from every nation, tribe and tongue. (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/21.htm)
- **“Kings of the earth”** — not literal earthly monarchs in a separate category, but language drawn from Isaiah 60:3 to convey that all authority and honour is now submitted to God. (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/21.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/21.htm)
- **Enduring Word** raises the question whether these “kings” are a distinct class of the redeemed or simply colourful language for the honour brought into the city. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-21/)

### v. 25 – “Its gates will never be shut at the end of the day, because there will be no night there.”

- **Perpetual access, perfect security.** In ancient cities, gates were shut at night for safety. Here there is no night and no enemy — the gates remain forever open. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-21/)
- **Fulfilment of Isaiah 60:11:** in the Millennium, Jerusalem’s gates were open day and night; in the eternal state, there is no night at all. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-21/)

### v. 26 – “And into the city will be brought the glory and honor of the nations.”

- **All that is genuinely good in human culture is brought in.** The Pulpit Commentary sees this as earthly symbolism: not that there will be literal kings and nations on a physical earth, but language conveying that all glory is now rightly ordered under God. (biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/21.htm)

### v. 27 – “But nothing unclean will ever enter it, nor anyone who practices an abomination or a lie, but only those whose names are written in the Lamb’s Book of Life.”

- **Absolute purity of the city.** Those excluded match the list in v.8 — the unrepentant sinners have no access. Entry is solely by being written in the Lamb’s Book of Life, i.e., by grace through faith. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/21.htm; enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-21/)
- **The Book of Life is the decisive register.** Ellicott: “Sin indeed excludes from the city, but it is sin loved, sin unrepented of, which alone can close the gate.” The open gates and the exclusive register stand together as both invitation and warning. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/21.htm)

## Where Protestant traditions differ (from the sources found)

- **Dispensational / premillennial** (Gill, Walvoord as cited in Enduring Word): The new heaven and earth of Rev 21 is the millennial kingdom on a renewed earth, not the final eternal state. The sea’s absence is a change in quality, not literal removal. The New Jerusalem is a real city, not merely the Church. (biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/revelation/21.htm; enduringword.com/bible-commentary/revelation-21/; studylight.org/commentary/revelation-21-2.html)
- **Amillennial / traditional Protestant** (Ellicott, Pulpit Commentary, Enduring Word’s main reading): Rev 21 depicts the eternal state — beyond the Millennium, beyond time. The city is both the Church and a real dwelling; the symbolism conveys spiritual realities that surpass literal description. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/revelation/21.htm; biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/revelation/21.htm)
- **Lutheran** (1517.org, LCMS): The vision is read through the lens of Christ’s mystical union with the Church. The “new Jerusalem” is the Church in glory. The 1,000 years of Rev 20 are figurative for the entire church age; Rev 21 is the final consummation at Christ’s one return. The Lutheran reading stresses present comfort: the hope of the resurrection transforms how believers see the world now. (1517.org/articles/epistle-revelation-211-17-easter-5-series-c-2025; 1517.org/articles/epistle-revelation-219-14-21-27-easter-6-series-c; reporter.lcms.org/2006/bible-study-evaluates-left-behind-theology/)
- **Baptist** (Spurgeon, Gill): Spurgeon preached “all things new” as sovereign grace: God alone makes the new creation; man contributes nothing. Gill’s historic Baptist reading is premillennial — the chapter describes the 1,000‑year reign of Christ on a renewed earth, not the ultimate heaven. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/revelation-21.html; biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/revelation/21.htm)
